title: Driving Without a Valid MOT: Fines, Points and Insurance Risk
excerpt: Driving without a valid MOT can cost up to £1,000, rising to £2,500 and points if the car has a dangerous defect - and it can void your insurance. Here's the full picture.
featuredAlt: Penalty for driving without an MOT
contentHtml:
Driving without a valid MOT can bring a fine of up to £1,000. If the car has a dangerous defect it rises to up to £2,500 plus 3 penalty points, and driving without an MOT can also invalidate your insurance. The only journeys allowed on an expired MOT are to a pre-booked MOT test or to a garage for repairs. Check any car's MOT status free on RegScan before you drive.

The fine for driving without an MOT

Using a vehicle on a public road without a valid MOT (where one is required) is an offence. The standard penalty is a fine of up to £1,000. It doesn't matter if the car is otherwise fine - if the MOT has lapsed and you drive it, you're committing the offence.

When it gets worse: dangerous defects

If you drive a vehicle with a dangerous defect (the most serious MOT category), the penalty rises to up to £2,500, 3 penalty points, and a possible driving ban. A dangerous defect is one that's an immediate risk to safety or the environment - so this is treated far more seriously than a simply-expired certificate.

Your insurance can be void too

Most insurers require your vehicle to be roadworthy and legal. Driving without a valid MOT can breach your policy terms, meaning a claim could be refused and you could be treated as uninsured - which is a separate, more serious offence with its own fine and points.

The only legal exceptions

You can drive a car with an expired MOT only:

  • to a pre-booked MOT test appointment, or
  • to or from a garage for repairs needed to pass the MOT.

Even then, the vehicle must be roadworthy and taxed/insured. "I was on my way to book it" is not a defence.

No MOT vs no tax: the penalties differ

No MOT and no tax are separate offences with separate penalties. Driving with no MOT risks a fine of up to £1,000 (up to £2,500 and points if there's a dangerous defect). Keeping or using a vehicle with no tax is enforced by the DVLA with an automatic penalty and possible clamping. Because you generally can't tax a car without a valid MOT, a lapsed MOT often leaves you exposed to both at once.

Do you get points for driving without an MOT?

Not for a simply-expired MOT on its own - that's a fine of up to £1,000 with no penalty points. Points come in when the car has a dangerous defect: that's where the up-to-£2,500 fine and 3 penalty points apply. So a lapsed certificate alone is a fine, not points - but driving something genuinely unsafe is treated far more harshly.

How likely are you to get caught?

Very. Police and DVSA use ANPR cameras linked to the MOT database that automatically flag vehicles without a valid MOT as they pass. Enforcement is largely automated, so an expired MOT is easy to detect on any journey.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the fine for driving without an MOT?

Up to £1,000 for driving a vehicle without a valid MOT. If it has a dangerous defect, up to £2,500 plus 3 penalty points and a possible ban.

Can I be fined if my car is just parked with no MOT?

No - the offence is driving/using it on a road. But a car kept on a public road must still be taxed, and you generally can't tax it without a valid MOT, so it should be declared SORN and kept off-road.

Does no MOT invalidate my insurance?

It can. Insurers usually require the vehicle to be roadworthy and legal, so driving without a valid MOT may let them refuse a claim.

Can I drive to get an MOT if mine has expired?

Yes, but only to a pre-booked MOT test, or to a garage for repairs needed to pass. The car must still be taxed, insured and roadworthy.

What are the penalties for driving without an MOT?

A fine of up to £1,000. If the vehicle has a dangerous defect, up to £2,500, 3 penalty points and a possible ban - plus your insurance can be voided.

Do you get penalty points for no MOT?

Not for a simply-expired MOT - that's a fine only. Penalty points (3) apply where the car has a dangerous defect.

What is the penalty for no MOT or no tax?

They're separate: no MOT is a fine of up to £1,000 (more with a dangerous defect); no tax is a DVLA penalty plus possible clamping. A lapsed MOT often triggers both, since you usually can't tax the car without one.
